items.ig_caption:
22 GitHub repos. Built to hijack your AI coding agent. 🤖

What Cyber Security News reported (18 Nov), from Bitdefender Labs:
→ Attackers planted poisoned files in GitHub repos so AI coding assistants would run hidden malware
→ Claude Code and Cursor are named targets; the malware looks for settings of 14 agents
→ It steals CI/CD, cloud and package-registry tokens, SSH keys, password-manager data and .env secrets
→ It then spreads through stolen GitHub and GitLab tokens
→ A second path uses session-start hooks that run a command without any AI prompt

My take: I'd treat a cloned repo like an email attachment now: check CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md and hook settings before any agent opens it, and keep long-lived tokens off dev laptops.

What to do: before opening an unfamiliar repo in an AI-enabled editor, check AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, the .claude/, .cursor/ and .gemini/ folders, MCP server definitions and setup scripts. If a machine ran one, rotate every token and secret it could reach.

cover.hook: One signed certificate. Code execution on your Puppet Server.
cover.sub: CISA says CVE-2026-115731 (CVSS 9.4) is exploited. Perforce fixes have been out since 3 Nov.

slides.title: The flaw
slides.body: CVE-2026-115731 (CVSS 9.4) is a deserialization flaw in Puppet report processing. Per CISA, any client holding a CA-signed agent certificate can run code as the service user on the Puppet Server.

slides.title: Why auto-signing matters
slides.body: An unauthenticated attacker can get such a certificate if the CA auto-signs without strong verification. Neodyme, who found it, says RCE lets an attacker take the CA signing keys and impersonate other hosts.

slides.label: CISA deadline for US federal agencies
slides.note: Added to KEV on 17 Nov. A second flaw, CVE-2026-115732 (CVSS 9.0), bypasses certificate-name authorization.

items.ig_caption:
One signed certificate. Code execution on your Puppet Server. ⚙️

What The Hacker News reported (18 Nov):
→ CISA added CVE-2026-115731 (CVSS 9.4), a Puppet deserialization flaw, to its exploited list (KEV) on 17 Nov
→ Per CISA, any client holding a CA-signed agent certificate can run code as the service user on the Puppet Server
→ An unauthenticated attacker can get such a certificate if the CA auto-signs without strong verification
→ Neodyme, who found it, says an attacker can then take the CA signing keys and impersonate other hosts
→ Perforce shipped fixes on 3 Nov; OpenVox is affected too

My take: Config management servers hold the keys to the whole fleet. I'd check CA auto-signing first, and if the Puppet Server was hit, assume the CA itself needs rotating.

What to do: update to Puppet Enterprise 2026.0.1, 2025.12.1 or 2023.8.13 (Core 9.1.3 / 8.22.2), OpenVox Server 9.2.0 / 8.18.0, and review CA auto-signing.

items.ig_caption:
$40.5 million in ransoms. Four arrests. 🚔

What BleepingComputer reported (18 Nov):
→ Ukraine's National Police and the FBI ran 66 searches in Kyiv and 11 regions; four suspected key members are in custody
→ Police say at least 28 companies paid more than $40.5 million in ransoms
→ Ukrainian court records identify Chaos as the ransomware used; the probe is ongoing
→ Police say the gang called staff posing as IT support, with AI-generated voice messages, fake corporate VPN pages and remote tools like AnyDesk
→ Seized: computers, phones, bank cards, about $370,000 and €20,000 in cash

My take: Help-desk impersonation beats most technical controls. I'd make call-backs non-negotiable: no remote session and no MFA reset until the caller is verified on a directory number.

What to do: publish one rule to all staff: IT never asks you to install a remote tool or log into a VPN link from a call. Hang up and call the help desk back.
